criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Intro links product-quality/public-safety ethics to engineering design and competitive organisational context; lists stakeholders. Stakeholder interests are only briefly noted, and several ethical issues are not fully described, so not Excellent.

evidence.quote: the issue of maintaining product quality safety while trying to succeed as a business in a competitive field.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Presents for (competitive advantage, revenue, jobs) and against (harm, code, reputation) and concludes not ship. Depth moderate; recommendations mostly for Rachel/company, not several stakeholders.

evidence.quote: While there is some merit to shipping the products, such as economic benefits and maintaining a competitive advantage

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logical structure moves from for/against to conclusion; conclusion supported by EACE and NHS/VW cases. Not systematic for all stakeholders (chip supplier, health department underdeveloped), so not Excellent.

evidence.quote: the short-term benefit trade-off is greatly outweighed by the potential risks of harm to end-users

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Uses relevant external cases (NHS, VW, Apple) and EACE, but only four references, several claims unsupported, no quantitative evidence, and references incomplete. Demonstrates moderate rather than in-depth research.

evidence.quote: In late 2023, the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) investigated a series ofIT system failures in NHS hospitals

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Has required sections and is mostly fluent, but contains typos/grammar errors, no figures/tables, and references are few and poorly formatted. Satisfactory.

technical_issues.issue: Large-scale testing to inform future safety improvements is not evaluated; the growth argument is speculative.
References incomplete/malformed (BBC lacks URL; CNBC URL corrupted; NYT author garbled), limiting verifiability.
Apple product-release example is weak evidence for shipping defective servers; not directly analogous.

overall: A well-structured ethics report with a clear not-ship recommendation and relevant cases, but it lacks a decision framework for shipping known-defect products, underdevelops several stakeholders, and has limited/incomplete evidence and references. Marks: C1 8, C2 8, C3 8, C4 6, C5 4.

feedback.summary: You wrote a well-structured ethics report with a clear not-ship recommendation and relevant cases. Your Introduction and balanced Discussion are strengths. To reach the next level, deepen stakeholder analysis, add a decision framework for shipping known-defect products, strengthen evidence with quantitative data and complete references, and improve presentation with proofreading and visual elements.
next_steps: Add a decision framework in the Discussion: specify risk severity/probability, disclosure, mitigation, and standards that determine when known-defect products may ship.
Deepen stakeholder analysis throughout: explain interests and recommendations for end users, Rachel, the company, the chip supplier, and the health department, not just Rachel/company.
Strengthen evidence and presentation: add quantitative data, complete/correct references, proofread grammar, and include at least one figure/table (e.g., stakeholder map or risk matrix).

criteria.C1: Your Introduction links product-quality and public-safety ethics to engineering design and the competitive organisational context, and you list stakeholders. To reach Excellent, describe several ethical issues with their significance and explain each stakeholder’s interests in more depth—especially end users, Rachel, the company, the chip supplier and the health department—so both context and stakeholder interest are clearly demonstrated.
criteria.C2: You present balanced for/against arguments (competitive advantage, revenue, jobs versus harm, codes, reputation) and conclude not to ship. To reach Excellent, add significant depth and make decision-making recommendations for several different stakeholders, not mainly Rachel/company. Also check that EACE 2.3b is applied to individual competence, not company resource or testing limits.
criteria.C3: Your report moves logically from for/against arguments to a conclusion supported by EACE and the NHS/VW cases. To reach Excellent, make the argument compelling and systematic for all stakeholders; the chip supplier and health department are underdeveloped. Integrate their perspectives throughout and show explicitly how each section supports your not-ship conclusion.
criteria.C4: You use relevant external cases (NHS, VW, Apple) and EACE, but evidence is limited to four references and several claims are unsupported. To reach Very good/Excellent, substantiate arguments with adequate references plus qualitative and quantitative evidence—e.g., defect severity, failure likelihood, recall costs—and complete/correct reference details so sources are verifiable.
criteria.C5: Your report has the required sections and is mostly fluent. To reach Good/Very good, proofread for grammar and spelling, use several types of visual elements competently (e.g., stakeholder map, risk matrix, decision flowchart), and provide consistently formatted, relevant references. This will improve clarity and support your discussion.
